papers.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: A fair, 132-run head-to-head test finds that ten self-distillation tricks for training AI agents rarely beat the simple GRPO baseline and usually cost more.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors retrain AI agents with ten popular "self-distillation" tricks under one fair, shared setup, and find that almost none of them reliably beat the plain, simpler baseline.

## Background you need
An agent here is a language model that acts step by step in an environment, like a text-based household game or an online shop. Reinforcement learning (training by trial, error and reward) teaches it which actions lead to success. The standard baseline is GRPO, a method that only rewards the agent at the end, based on whether the whole attempt worked. Self-distillation adds a "teacher" copy of the same model that sees extra hints during training, and uses its opinions to grade each individual step.

## The problem
New self-distillation papers appear at roughly one every two days. Each claims gains, but each uses its own environments, settings and evaluation. Many reuse baseline scores copied from older papers. So nobody knows which ideas really help. Teams training agents waste money and GPU time chasing methods that may only look good on paper.

## The idea
The paper acts like a consumer testing lab. Instead of trusting each manufacturer's brochure, it buys all ten products and tests them side by side, on the same bench, many times over. It then checks not only the final score, but also how bumpy the ride was and how much each method cost to run.

## How it works
1. **Pick the methods.** Ten self-distillation methods are grouped by how they use the teacher: as an extra training loss, as a way to boost or dampen step-level credit, as reward shaping, or by checking the teacher's suggested continuations.
2. **Fix the playing field.** All methods share the same four tasks: ALFWorld (household chores in text), ScienceWorld (science experiments in text), Search-QA (answering questions with a search tool) and WebShop (online shopping). Each method keeps the settings from its original paper and code.
3. **Train at three sizes.** Every method is trained on Qwen3.5 models with 2, 4 and 9 billion parameters, giving 12 model-task combinations. That is 132 runs of 100 training steps each.
4. **Measure carefully.** Final scores are averaged over eight separate runs of the agent (seeds). The team also tracks validation every five steps and records real training time. The whole study used about 12,124 GPU-hours on H800 chips.

## Results
GRPO averages 49.68 across the 12 settings. Only two methods beat that average: PCSD at 54.26 and AgentOPSD at 51.34. The other eight fall below the simple baseline. No method wins consistently; the leader changes with task and model size. PCSD has the best average yet leads no single setting.

Win counts can mislead. ICSD beats GRPO in seven of twelve settings, but one of its runs ends at 0% success. Training is often unstable: nine runs ended at least 20 points below their own peak.

Extra cost rarely pays off. In 112 of 120 comparisons, the self-distillation method needed more training time than GRPO, and 58 of those also scored lower. When given only GRPO's time budget, AgentOPSD dropped from 68.10% to 37.63% on the household task, below GRPO's 58.10%.

## Why it matters
Teams building agents can save compute by starting with the simple baseline. The paper also sets a reporting standard: show variation across runs, full training curves and measured cost, and rerun baselines yourself.

## Caveats
Only ten methods were covered, chosen for limited compute and time. Each method used its original paper's settings, which may not be its best possible configuration on these tasks. All tests used one model family and 100 training steps; longer training or other models could change the picture.

## Key terms
- **Agent:** a model that takes a series of actions in an environment to reach a goal.
- **Reinforcement learning:** training by letting a model try things and rewarding good outcomes.
- **GRPO:** a common baseline that scores a group of attempts by their final outcome only.
- **Self-distillation:** using a hint-aware copy of the same model as a teacher for each step.
- **Seed:** one independent repeat of a run, used to measure how much results vary.

papers.title: Data World: Scaling Data Environments from Scratch
papers.tldr: Data World generates synthetic data worlds from a known hidden blueprint so data-analysis agents can be trained and graded on checkable insights, boosting a 35B model on several outside benchmarks.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Data World builds fake-but-realistic data worlds from a written blueprint, so data-analysis agents can be trained and graded against a known hidden truth.

## Background you need
A data agent is a language model that reads files such as spreadsheets, writes analysis code and reports findings. Training it with reinforcement learning (rewarding good outcomes) requires many practice tasks plus a reliable way to check answers. A rubric is a checklist of points a good answer should contain. Synthetic data means data generated by a program rather than collected from the real world.

## The problem
Real business data is expensive to gather and often locked by privacy or ownership rules. Even when it exists, nobody knows the true process that produced it. So when an agent claims "sales dropped because of shipping delays", there is no ground truth to check it against. Rubrics written by browsing the files only reward what the rubric author happened to notice. Feedback ends up noisy.

## The idea
Think of a mystery-novel writer who decides the culprit and every clue before writing the book. Data World does the same: it first writes down the hidden causes and effects of a world, then generates the messy files from it. Because the "culprit" is known, every finding in an agent's report can be checked against what really caused the data.

## How it works
1. **Draft a cause-and-effect map.** Starting from a persona (for example, a regional retailer), the system builds a graph of which factors drive which others.
2. **Write a world contract.** A contract agent fixes the entities, timelines, the rule on each cause-effect link, global invariants (facts that must always hold) and the deliverables.
3. **Generate the hidden truth, then mess it up.** Agents build the clean hidden data layer by layer, with fixed random seeds. A separate step then adds real-world mess: inconsistent IDs, missing values, duplicates, unit changes and unlabeled links between tables.
4. **Audit and write tasks.** An independent auditor can only pass or fail a world; it cannot edit it. Each task asks the agent to explain a target factor's causes or trace its consequences. Rubrics split into "computation" items and "insight discovery" items, grounded in the known mechanism.
5. **Train.** The team runs reinforcement learning on the synthetic tasks with rubric scores as rewards, without copying solutions from stronger models.

## Results
The test set, DataWorld-Bench, has 100 tasks from 50 held-out worlds across 16 domains. The training set has 2,135 tasks from 1,037 separate worlds. Ten frontier models were tested. The best overall was GPT-6-Astra at 74.43 out of 100; the lowest scored 49.75. Every model scored lower on insight than on computation, with gaps from 4.87 to 21.35 points. In plain terms, models can crunch numbers better than they can explain what the numbers mean.

Training Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on the synthetic worlds produced DataWorld-35B-A3B. Compared with its base model, it gained 7.06 points on DataWorld-Bench. More telling, it also improved on outside benchmarks it never trained on: 14.28 points on DAComp, 20.90 on DABstep-Hard and 12.13 on JobBench.

## Why it matters
Companies that want analysis agents rarely can share real customer data for training. Data World offers a privacy-safe supply of practice worlds with checkable answers. The gains on outside benchmarks suggest skills learned in fake worlds carry over to real analysis tasks.
## Caveats
The designed mechanisms, rubric choices and the AI judge all carry biases. A valid insight that is not on the rubric gets no credit, which may understate some models. Per-domain task counts are too small to rank models within a single domain. Worlds were built with one model in one agent harness, so diversity depends on that generator.

## Key terms
- **Data agent:** a model that analyzes files by writing and running code.
- **Rubric:** a checklist used to score a written answer.
- **Hidden truth:** the clean, known process behind the generated files.
- **Audit:** an independent pass/fail check that the world behaves as designed.
- **Reinforcement learning:** training by rewarding good outcomes rather than copying examples.

papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: A training-free trick that keeps recent text in exact order and lumps older text into one sharpened memory, restoring and boosting speculative-decoding speed-ups on inputs up to 256K tokens.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
FOLD is a training-free fix that lets a small "draft" model keep helping a large model generate text fast, even when the input is hundreds of thousands of words long.

## Background you need
Speculative decoding speeds up a large language model by letting a small drafter model guess several next tokens (word pieces), which the big model then checks all at once. If the guesses are good, many tokens are accepted per step, so the reply comes out faster with identical output. Acceptance length is how many guessed tokens get accepted per round. Position encoding is how a model knows the order of words, by tagging each one with its distance from the current point.

## The problem
Long inputs, such as whole codebases or long reports, are exactly where speed-ups matter most. But drafters are usually trained on short texts. On long inputs they see distances they never saw in training, and their attention (how they spread focus over earlier text) gets diluted across too many tokens. For one popular drafter on Llama-3.1-8B, the speed-up nearly halves within 32,000 tokens. Retraining drafters for long text costs data and compute for every model pair.

## The idea
Think of a student taking notes in a long lecture. They remember the last few minutes word for word, in order. Everything earlier goes into one notebook, where the order matters less than finding the relevant page. FOLD gives the drafter the same habit: exact order for recent text, and one "far memory" bin for everything older. A probe showed the model's internal features already carry order for far-apart tokens, so exact distances are not needed there.

## How it works
1. **Keep a local window.** The most recent tokens (2,048 or 4,096 of them) keep their exact positions, so short-range grammar and order stay intact.
2. **Fold everything older into far memory.** All older tokens are placed at one shared position just past the window. Nothing is thrown away, and the drafter never sees an unfamiliar distance.
3. **Sharpen the far memory.** Inside the far memory, attention is made "peakier", so it focuses on the few most relevant old tokens instead of spreading thinly.
4. **Balance the two parts.** The total influence of far memory grows much more slowly than its size, so a huge pile of old text cannot drown out the recent window. If the input fits in the window, FOLD behaves exactly like the original drafter.

## Results
Tests used six target-drafter pairs, including Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-8B, on inputs up to about 256,000 tokens. Speed-up is measured against normal one-token-at-a-time decoding on one H100 GPU.

On average, Llama-3.1-8B went from 2.11× to 3.40× faster. Qwen3.5-9B went from 2.98× to 3.39×, and Gemma-4-12B from 2.46× to 2.68×. On long code inputs of 122,000 tokens, Llama's speed-up rose from 2.08× to 4.22×. In practice, a reply that took 42 seconds without speculation now takes about 10 instead of 20. FOLD mostly beat other training-free methods such as StreamingLLM, YaRN and ReRoPE. In the SGLang serving system, Llama's speed-up rose from 1.54× to 2.50×.

## Why it matters
Coding assistants and document tools often feed models very long inputs. FOLD lets existing drafters keep their speed there without any retraining, and it does not change the big model's output. It works inside vLLM and SGLang.

## Caveats
Gains vary a lot by model and task; Gemma-4-12B improved only modestly. FOLD cannot fix cases where the big model itself struggles at long lengths. It was tested only on drafters that guess a whole block at once, not on step-by-step drafters like EAGLE-3. It keeps an extra memory copy that grows with input length, which may hurt under tight memory or many users. The window size and sharpening level are set by hand.

## Key terms
- **Speculative decoding:** a small model guesses tokens; the big model verifies them in one pass.
- **Drafter:** the small, fast guessing model.
- **Acceptance length:** how many guessed tokens are accepted per round.
- **Position encoding:** how a model tracks the order and distance of words.
- **Attention dilution:** focus getting spread too thin over very long inputs.

papers.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.tldr: RoLaQ learns a rotation and rounding range to store DeepSeek-style latent KV caches at 2 bits, fitting about 4x more context per GPU with smaller accuracy loss than prior 2-bit methods.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
RoLaQ shrinks the short-term memory of DeepSeek-style language models to 2 bits per number while keeping most of their accuracy, letting one GPU hold about four times more context.

## Background you need
While a model reads and writes, it stores a KV cache (its short-term memory of what it has already read). This cache grows with every token and often fills the GPU. Multi-head latent attention, used in DeepSeek models, already compresses that memory into one shared summary vector per token, called a latent. Quantization means storing numbers with fewer bits, like rounding prices to the nearest dollar, to save memory.

## The problem
Long conversations, documents and reasoning traces make the KV cache huge, which limits how many users a GPU can serve. Squeezing the cache to 2 bits saves a lot of memory, but the rounding errors are large. In latent attention, one shared latent feeds both the keys (which decide where to look) and the values (what gets read out). So one rounding error damages both jobs at once.
## The idea
Imagine packing a suitcase with fixed-size compartments. If you rotate the items so the most important ones lie along the roomiest directions, and choose compartment sizes that fit, far less gets crushed. RoLaQ learns a better "rotation" of the latent before rounding, and learns how wide the rounding range should be, while leaving the model itself untouched.

## How it works
1. **Find the directions that matter.** The method measures which latent directions carry the most energy for both keys and values, and splits them into two groups.
2. **Learn a rotation.** It learns a small adjustment to an existing rotation method (OSCAR) within each group. This uses half the parameters of a full rotation.
3. **Learn the rounding range.** For each layer it learns a cutoff for how large a value can be before clipping. A matched scale factor is tied to that cutoff, so the signal's overall strength stays the same after rounding.
4. **Calibrate briefly.** Using 1.43 million text tokens, it trains only these settings so the compressed model's predictions match the full-precision model. This takes about 22 to 34 minutes on one A100 GPU.
5. **Serve.** The rotation is folded into existing weights, and the cache stores packed 2-bit codes. A small position-related key part stays at full precision.

## Results
Tests used DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Moonlight-16B-A3B and MiniCPM3-4B across six tasks covering knowledge, trivia, math and code. Without any special protection for recent tokens, RoLaQ beat the strongest 2-bit baseline by 3.8, 2.8 and 1.1 points. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite math (GSM8K), accuracy rose from 18.3 with OSCAR to 32.1. Full precision is still higher: for example 49.4 versus RoLaQ's 46.7 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite.

On long-context retrieval at 16,000 tokens, RoLaQ scored 73.7, versus 67.4 for the best baseline and 84.7 for full precision. In serving on one A100, the same memory held 4.56 million tokens instead of 1.15 million, a 3.96× increase. Decoding with 256,000-token inputs ran 2.51× faster (67.7 versus 27.0 tokens per second). The slowest first-token wait at 256 concurrent users fell by 37.8%.

## Why it matters
Serving long-context models is limited by memory, not just compute. Fitting four times more context per GPU means more users per machine or much longer documents at the same cost. Frozen weights and minutes of calibration make it cheap to apply.

## Caveats
There is still a clear accuracy gap to full precision, especially on long retrieval. Short inputs can actually run slower (0.88× at 1,000 tokens) due to packing overhead. Speed was measured only on one model and one GPU type; other hardware needs custom code. The position-related key part and grouping metadata remain uncompressed.

## Key terms
- **KV cache:** the model's stored memory of earlier tokens, reused for each new token.
- **Latent attention:** a design that stores one compressed vector per token instead of full keys and values.
- **Quantization:** storing numbers with fewer bits to save memory.
- **Calibration:** briefly tuning a few settings on sample text, without retraining the model.
- **Throughput:** how many tokens the system produces per second.

papers.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
papers.tldr: KronLSTM is a linear-attention model whose memory update corrects one key-value link at a time, staying stable without extra normalization and beating Gated DeltaNet-style rivals on long-context tests.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors design a new memory-update rule for fast "linear attention" language models that fixes one stored fact at a time without smudging the others, and it beats strong rivals on long-context tests.

## Background you need
Standard Transformers compare every word with every earlier word, so cost grows with the square of length. Linear attention models instead squeeze everything they have read into one fixed-size table of numbers, called the memory matrix. Reading and writing that table costs the same at word 10 or word 100,000. The "delta rule" is a popular way to write into this table: it looks at what the memory currently predicts and nudges it toward the right answer.

## The problem
If nothing limits a fixed-size memory, its numbers can grow without bound and training becomes unstable. The xLSTM family adds extra bookkeeping states, but these can still cause sudden gradient spikes. Delta-rule models such as Gated DeltaNet stay bounded. But each correction can disturb other stored items whose keys (the "addresses" used for lookup) overlap with the new one. Over a long document, these disturbances pile up and recall suffers.

## The idea
Think of a filing cabinet with labeled drawers. The usual delta rule rewrites a whole drawer, and anything filed under a similar label gets bumped too. The Kronecker Delta Rule fixes only the single label-and-content pairing that is wrong. Another item is disturbed only if both its label and its content resemble the new one.

## How it works
1. Each token produces a query, a key and a value. These are normalized to unit length, so no single update can blow up the memory.
2. Instead of correcting the whole value stored for a key, the rule corrects one number: how strongly this key is linked to this value. An erase gate removes the old link and a write gate sets the new strength.
3. A forget gate lets old information fade when it is no longer useful.
4. The model, called KronLSTM, needs none of the extra stabilizer states that earlier xLSTM layers used.
5. The authors prove that the memory's expected size stays bounded over any sequence length.

## Results
The authors trained 1.5-billion-parameter models on 100 billion tokens of web text. Baselines included Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Mamba-3, Gated DeltaNet-2 and mLSTM.
- On six common-sense and reading tests, pure KronLSTM averaged 59.72, against 58.12 for the best rival, Kimi Delta Attention.
- On the LAMBADA word-prediction test, its perplexity (a measure of surprise; lower is better) was 11.72, against 12.58 for Gated DeltaNet.
- After extending the context to 32,000 tokens, it scored 60.19 on average against 58.75 for Gated DeltaNet-2. Perplexity was 7.66 against 8.36.
- On needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, it was best or second-best at 4,000 to 16,000 tokens on all but one task. On the multi-query task, its lead grew from 2.4 to 4.1 points as length grew.
- On one H100 GPU, it trained at 36,800 to 44,500 tokens per second. That is 11–18% faster than Gated DeltaNet-2, though plain Gated DeltaNet stayed faster.

## Why it matters
Long documents, codebases and chat histories are where linear models should shine, since their memory cost stays flat. A write rule that disturbs less old information could make them better at finding details buried deep in a long input. Code and models are public.

## Caveats
No model exceeded 1.5 billion parameters. Many gaps are under one point, from single runs without error bars. KronLSTM underperforms on one synthetic retrieval task with repeated noise sentences. It is slower than plain Gated DeltaNet. Hybrids with full attention layers are future work.

## Key terms
- **Linear attention**: a Transformer variant that stores context in a fixed-size memory, so cost grows only linearly with length.
- **Delta rule**: an update that nudges memory toward the correct answer based on its current prediction error.
- **Key / value**: the lookup address and the stored content for each token.
- **Perplexity**: how surprised a model is by real text; lower is better.
- **Needle-in-a-haystack**: a test that hides one fact in a long text and asks the model to find it.

papers.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
papers.tldr: Running the Muon optimizer on small blocks of structured (Monarch) weight matrices cuts optimizer memory by about half and speeds up a 6.89B model's training step by about 45%.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The paper combines a cheap, structured way of storing a model's weight matrices with the Muon optimizer, making pretraining faster and lighter on memory while keeping most of the quality.

## Background you need
An optimizer is the rule that decides how to change a model's weights after each training step. AdamW, the standard choice, keeps two extra numbers for every weight, so its "optimizer state" can rival the model itself in size. Muon is a newer optimizer that treats each weight matrix as a whole and "orthogonalizes" its update, which roughly means balancing the step evenly across all directions. A Monarch matrix is a large matrix built from a few small square blocks plus fixed shuffles, so it has far fewer free numbers than a full matrix.

## The problem
Training large language models is limited by GPU memory and time. Memory-saving optimizers such as GaLore shrink the optimizer state but keep full-size weights and gradients. Muon often trains better than AdamW, but its orthogonalization is expensive for big matrices and may need extra communication across GPUs. The open question: do Muon's benefits survive when weights are stored in a compact structured form?

## The idea
Picture tidying one huge warehouse versus a row of small rooms. Each room is quick, and rooms can be done side by side. Monarch-Muon splits each big weight matrix into small blocks and runs Muon's balancing step on each block separately. The authors prove Muon's underlying math problem genuinely breaks apart block by block.

## How it works
1. Each chosen weight matrix is written as a product of two block-diagonal pieces with fixed shuffles between them. The full dense matrix is never built, even in the forward pass.
2. Every small block keeps its own momentum buffer, a running average of recent gradients.
3. Each block's momentum is orthogonalized with a few Newton–Schulz steps, a cheap repeated multiplication that approximates the balanced direction.
4. Blocks of the same shape are batched together, so the GPU handles many small problems in one go.
5. Parts that are not Monarch-structured, such as embeddings, normalization layers and mixture-of-experts routers, still use AdamW.

## Results
The authors tested a 257-million-parameter dense model on about 5.1 billion tokens and a mixture-of-experts model on about 7.34 billion tokens.
- At the same structure, Monarch-Muon beat Monarch-AdamW in all four comparisons. For the dense model with two blocks, validation loss was 3.06 versus 3.09.
- The two-block mixture-of-experts version matched dense AdamW's loss of 2.68. It used 767 million total parameters instead of 1.029 billion, about 25% fewer.
- On a 6.89-billion-parameter model on one H100 GPU, peak memory fell from 68.87 to 52.94 GB. Optimizer state shrank from 14.60 to 6.77 GB.
- The optimizer step ran about 4.2 times faster, from 1,288 to 304 milliseconds. A full training step fell from about 2.99 to 1.64 seconds, roughly 45% faster.
- Using 8-bit number formats on top cut peak memory by about 31% and step time by 14%, with loss within 0.23% of the usual 16-bit setup.

## Why it matters
Memory and step time decide how big a model a lab can train and how long it takes. Halving optimizer memory and nearly halving step time at the 7-billion scale could let smaller teams pretrain larger models.

## Caveats
Structured weights still lose some quality in the dense setting: dense Muon reached 2.99 loss against 3.06. At the smallest size, Monarch-Muon was actually slower than dense Muon. Quality runs are single runs at modest scale, and long multi-GPU runs remain untested. The convergence proof assumes exact orthogonalization, not the few cheap steps used in practice.

## Key terms
- **Optimizer state**: extra numbers an optimizer keeps per weight, such as running averages of gradients.
- **Muon**: an optimizer that balances each matrix update across all directions before applying it.
- **Monarch matrix**: a large matrix built from small blocks and fixed shuffles, with far fewer free numbers.
- **Mixture of experts**: a model with many sub-networks where each token uses only a few of them.
- **Validation loss**: the error on held-out text; lower means better predictions.

papers.title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
papers.tldr: MCCL watches real GPU-to-GPU link speeds during training and, when a link silently slows, re-plans and hot-swaps communication schedules in milliseconds, cutting simulated training time by up to 4.99x.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
MCCL is a communication library for multi-GPU training that keeps measuring how fast each link really is, and when a link quietly slows down, it redesigns and swaps in a better data-sharing plan in milliseconds without stopping training.

## Background you need
Large models are trained on thousands of GPUs that constantly exchange data through "collectives," group operations such as AllGather (everyone collects everyone's piece) or AllToAll (everyone sends a different piece to everyone). Libraries such as NVIDIA's NCCL decide the route each chunk of data takes; that plan is called a schedule. A "gray failure" is hardware that still works but runs slower than it should, for example an overheating chip or a flaky network card.

## The problem
Today's libraries compute a plan once, assuming every link runs at full speed. Gray failures break that assumption and can last long; the paper cites about 72 minutes on average for congestion cases. Training repeats the same collectives thousands of times, so one slow link drags down every step. In a 16-GPU simulation, re-planning around one slowed link gave up to 7.1 times better performance than the static plan.

## The idea
Think of a delivery company with fixed routes. If one bridge is half-closed, every truck still queues at it. MCCL is a dispatcher who watches real delivery times, spots the slow bridge, and hands drivers new routes between trips.

## How it works
1. **Passive measurement.** MCCL times the real training transfers instead of sending test traffic. Inside a server, small counters in GPU memory record throughput; between servers, the CPU helper process does it. Results go to a central controller.
2. **Diagnosis.** The controller smooths the readings to ignore brief bursts. It checks whether a slowdown sits on the links that actually limit each schedule. Only schedules that are truly hurt get flagged.
3. **Warm-started re-planning.** For flagged collectives, an optimizer recomputes the schedule starting from the previous solution rather than from scratch. This is much faster.
4. **Hot-swap.** The new plan is loaded in the background. GPUs briefly agree on which collective number will be the first to use it, so old operations finish on the old plan and new ones use the new plan.

## Results
- On a real prototype with eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs across two servers, measurement error stayed below 1.2%. Overhead was about 2% when the fast in-server links were saturated, and below 1% at default settings.
- When one link between servers was halved, AllGather bandwidth fell from 74.0 to 44.8 GB per second. MCCL detected the problem in 53 milliseconds, re-planned in 13 milliseconds and swapped in about 12 milliseconds. Bandwidth then recovered to 59.7 GB per second.
- Warm-starting made AllToAll re-planning up to 18.3 times faster, with solutions for 512-GPU collectives within tens of seconds.
- In simulated training of Llama 3.1 405B and DeepSeek-V3 671B under gray failures, MCCL cut training time by up to 2.85 times and 4.99 times respectively, compared with plain NCCL. A job that would take five days could finish in about one.

## Why it matters
At large scale, something is almost always running slow. Turning a silent multi-hour slowdown into a sub-second fix, without restarting training, could save significant GPU time for any lab training big models.

## Caveats
The big end-to-end speedups come from simulation, not real clusters, and the hardware test used only eight GPUs. With healthy hardware, MCCL gave no gain on the tested network layout. It focuses on AllGather and AllToAll; reduction steps stay static. Detection thresholds need per-cluster tuning, and protection against flip-flopping between plans is future work. In-server overhead can reach about 13% with very few parallel channels and small chunks. It also depends on modifying NCCL internals.

## Key terms
- **Collective**: a group data-exchange operation among many GPUs, such as AllGather or AllToAll.
- **Schedule**: the plan for which data travels over which link, and when.
- **Gray failure**: a component that still works but is silently slower than normal.
- **Warm start**: solving a new problem by starting from the previous solution instead of from scratch.
- **Hot-swap**: replacing a running component without stopping the system.

papers.title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
papers.tldr: AMD's Primus Projection predicts multi-node training speed from single-GPU measurements within about 10%, letting an AI agent find a Mixtral 8x22B setup about 27% faster in under 30 minutes.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Primus Projection predicts how fast and how memory-hungry a large training job will be on hundreds of GPUs using just one or a few GPUs, and an AI agent uses those predictions to search for the best training setup in minutes instead of days.

## Background you need
Training a large language model spreads work across many GPUs in several ways at once. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's math, pipeline parallelism splits layers into stages, and expert parallelism spreads mixture-of-experts sub-networks across GPUs. Engineers must also pick the micro-batch size (how many examples each GPU handles at once) and recomputation (re-doing some math to save memory). The combination is called a configuration, and the right one can change speed a lot.

## The problem
These settings interact, so tuning one at a time misses good combinations. Teams mostly guess, launch multi-node jobs, wait, and adjust. Each try can tie up hundreds of GPUs for tens of minutes, and many end in out-of-memory crashes.

## The idea
It is like a flight simulator for training jobs. Instead of flying every new route with a real plane, you measure a few key parts on the ground and simulate the full trip. Once the simulator is fast and roughly right, you can try hundreds of routes and only fly the most promising ones.

## How it works
1. **Measure small.** The projection engine runs microbenchmarks (short timing tests of the real math kernels and communication) on as little as one GPU.
2. **Scale up on paper.** A "downscale, measure, upscale" workflow analytically estimates what it cannot measure locally: communication across many servers, overlap of sharded weights, and the full pipeline timeline. A CPU-only mode allows planning with no GPUs at all.
3. **Filter impossible options.** A memory model rejects configurations that would run out of GPU memory before any GPU time is spent.
4. **Search systematically.** A plain planner first sweeps one setting at a time from the user's starting point.
5. **Let an AI agent explore.** A large language model then proposes combinations across several settings, scores them in seconds with the projector, and keeps notes between rounds. Only top candidates get real hardware runs.

## Results
- Projections stayed within about 10% of measured multi-node speed for Llama 3.1 (a dense model) and Mixtral 8x22B (a mixture-of-experts model) across two GPU generations.
- The error was 4.7% for DeepSeek-V3 671B on 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% for Qwen3-235B on 256 GPUs.
- Scoring a candidate takes seconds instead of tens of minutes on real hardware.
- In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the agent found a setup about 27% faster than a published four-node reference, after under 30 minutes of single-node exploration. In practice, a run that took four days would take a little over three.
- AMD's companion blog post on the same tool adds detail for that case on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. The reference reached 3,475 tokens per second per GPU, and the best setup measured 4,402. The memory filter rejected 7 of 30 candidates, saving roughly 175 GPU-minutes.

## Why it matters
Cluster time is one of the largest costs in AI. A trustworthy predictor lets teams plan hardware purchases, catch memory problems early, and start big runs with a good configuration instead of burning days on trial runs.

## Caveats
I could not read the full paper text; details beyond the abstract come from AMD's companion blog post. The roughly 10% error is acceptable only if it is a steady bias that keeps the ranking of configurations correct. Memory estimates can miss peak usage, so settings near the limit still need a real check. The search is heuristic, not exhaustive. Agent results may vary with the language model used.

## Key terms
- **Configuration**: the full set of choices for splitting and running a training job across GPUs.
- **Microbenchmark**: a short, focused timing test of one operation.
- **Pipeline parallelism**: splitting a model's layers into stages that run on different GPUs.
- **Mixture of experts**: a model with many sub-networks, where each token uses only a few.
- **Throughput**: how much training data the system processes per second.

papers.title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
papers.tldr: Giving robot policies a side task of predicting future visual features, even with half or less of training spent on actions, beats action-only training in simulation and on a real arm.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper shows that robot policies often learn better when part of their training time goes to predicting what the scene will look like next, instead of spending all of it on predicting motor commands.

## Background you need
A vision-language-action model (a robot brain that reads camera images and a text instruction and outputs arm movements) is usually trained by imitation: it copies recorded human demonstrations. Besides the actions themselves, it can also be asked to predict "auxiliary targets" (extra side tasks that are not the final output). Two popular side tasks are latent actions (a compressed description of how the scene changed between frames) and future vision (a feature summary of the next camera image).

## The problem
Most teams pour nearly all training samples into predicting actions, and treat side tasks as optional extras. Nobody had cleanly tested how to split a fixed training budget between actions and side tasks. Past comparisons also mixed different architectures, data and settings, so it was hard to know what actually helped.

## The idea
Think of a student preparing for a driving test. Practicing only the steering wheel helps, but also asking "what will the road look like in two seconds?" builds understanding that makes the steering better. The authors ask which kind of "imagine the future" homework helps most, and how much of the study time it deserves.

## How it works
1. They build one shared model. A vision-language backbone (MiniCPM-V-4.6) feeds two expert streams: one predicts actions, one predicts an auxiliary target. The two streams talk through shared attention (a mechanism that lets each part look at the other's information).
2. A sample-level router sends each training example to exactly one job: the action loss or the side-task loss. A setting like "P50" means half the samples go to actions; "P100" means actions only.
3. They test three latent-action targets, built from raw pixel changes or from changes in DINO features (a widely used pretrained image representation).
4. They test three future-vision targets: features from DINOv3, from V-JEPA 2 (a video model), and from the Wan2.2 video autoencoder.
5. They evaluate on two simulated benchmarks, LIBERO and CALVIN, and four real tasks on one robot arm, with matched sample budgets.

## Results
On LIBERO, action-only training at full budget scored 96.5% average success. With half the samples moved to future vision, Wan2.2 targets reached 98.15% and V-JEPA 2 reached 97.95%. On CALVIN, scored by how many chained tasks the robot completes in a row (out of five), action-only got 4.314. V-JEPA 2 reached 4.451, and the best latent-action target reached 4.434.

Allocation surprised the authors. On CALVIN, V-JEPA 2 with only a quarter of samples on actions hit 4.522, beating its action-only control at 4.091. On LIBERO, though, every quarter-split setting fell below its control.

On the real robot, gains were largest. For a pick-out task scored out of 160, action-only got 116 and Wan2.2 got 156. Every future-vision setting beat action-only on all four tasks, while no latent-action setting did.

Probing tests suggest why. Future-vision features encode where things are and which task is running. Latent-action features encode relative motion.

## Why it matters
The finding gives robot teams a cheap lever: change what the model predicts, not how big it is. It also argues that the field's default of action-heavy training is a choice worth testing.

## Caveats
Budgets were matched by number of samples, not by compute or wall-clock time. Most tables report a single random seed; multi-seed numbers exist only for CALVIN. The real-robot tests used one arm and four tasks. The best split depends on the benchmark, so there is no universal recipe. The probing analysis shows correlations, not proven causes.

## Key terms
- **Vision-language-action model**: a model that turns images and instructions into robot movements.
- **Auxiliary target**: an extra prediction task used only to improve learning.
- **Latent action**: a compact code describing how a scene changed between two moments.
- **Future vision**: predicting a feature summary of an upcoming camera frame.
- **Sample router**: a rule deciding which training job each example serves.

papers.title: Residual Modeling Closes the Regression and Generative Policy Gap in Robot Learning
papers.tldr: A one-step robot policy trained with an outlier-tolerant error model matches or beats slower flow-matching policies on several benchmarks while running up to 18 times faster.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper explains why simple "predict the average action" robot policies lose to fancier generative ones, and fixes it with a smarter error model that is nearly twice as fast at run time.

## Background you need
A robot policy maps what the robot sees to what it should do next, often as an action chunk (a short sequence of future movements). Regression policies predict that chunk directly, trained with mean squared error (a loss that punishes the squared distance between guess and target). Generative policies, such as diffusion or flow matching (methods that build an answer by gradually refining random noise), are slower but usually score higher.

## The problem
The common story is that demonstrations are "multimodal": a person might go left or right around an obstacle, and averaging gives a useless middle path. Generative models can represent both options. But that story may be incomplete. Generative policies need many refinement steps, which slows control loops and training. If a one-step regression model could match them, robots would react faster and cost less to train.

## The idea
The authors looked at residuals (the leftover gap between the model's guess and the true action) in real robot data. Two things stood out. Some situations are inherently noisier than others. And a few errors are very large, far more than a bell curve predicts. Squared error lets those rare huge errors dominate learning, like a teacher who grades the whole class based on the two worst exams.

## How it works
1. They measured residuals on four datasets, including Bridge and Fractal, and confirmed varying noise levels and heavy tails.
2. They showed that squared-error training concentrates gradient signal (the push that updates the model) on a few high-error examples.
3. Their fix, HT-Policies, swaps squared error for a Student-t likelihood (an error model that expects occasional large mistakes and gives them less weight).
4. The network also predicts its own uncertainty for each situation, so noisy moments are treated as noisy.
5. It runs in one forward pass. It can reuse existing pretrained flow-matching models such as pi-0.5 or GR00T by fixing their noise input and adding a small uncertainty head.

## Results
On RoboCasa-GR1 trained from scratch, success was 5.8% for squared error, 14.0% for flow matching, and 33.5% for HT-Policies. When fine-tuning GR00T on RoboCasa-GR1, HT reached 50.01% versus 42.34% for flow matching. On SIMPLER Bridge it matched flow (62.31% vs 62.06%). On SIMPLER Fractal it trailed (65.25% vs 67.83%). Across five fine-tuning settings, HT beat plain squared error every time and beat flow in three.

Speed gains were clear on an RTX 5090 GPU. GR00T went from 46 to 25 milliseconds per decision, a 1.88 times speed-up. Pi-0.5 went from 124 to 68 milliseconds. Cosmos3-Nano went from 1,272 to 71 milliseconds, about 18 times faster. That means a robot can react about 14 times per second instead of less than once.

On three real tasks with 100 demonstrations each, HT largely closed the gap with generative policies. The paper gives these real-robot numbers only in a figure. HT also reached strong success in fewer training steps.

## Why it matters
Faster decisions mean smoother, safer robot motion and cheaper hardware. The work also reframes a debate: part of the generative advantage comes from how errors are handled, not just from modeling multiple choices. Teams could retrofit existing large robot models for quicker inference.

## Caveats
HT-Policies cannot represent several distinct options, so truly multimodal tasks still need generative models. The analysis does not link error statistics directly to closed-loop failures. Reinforcement learning use was only lightly tested. Results were not uniformly better; Fractal favored flow matching.

## Key terms
- **Action chunk**: a short planned sequence of future robot movements.
- **Residual**: the gap between a predicted action and the demonstrated one.
- **Heavy tails**: rare but very large errors occur more than a bell curve expects.
- **Student-t likelihood**: an error model that tolerates outliers by downweighting them.
- **Flow matching**: a generative method that refines noise into an answer over several steps.

papers.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
papers.tldr: An RL-trained builder model reorganizes documents into a linked folder workspace ahead of time, lifting a separate model's accuracy on hard multi-document questions from about 44% to 75%.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper trains a "librarian" AI that reorganizes a pile of documents into a well-linked folder system before any questions arrive, so a second AI can answer hard questions far more accurately.

## Background you need
Large language models struggle when the answer is spread across many long documents. The usual fix is retrieval-augmented generation (fetching a few relevant passages for each question). Another is precomputing a knowledge graph (a fixed network of entities and relations). Reinforcement learning (training by trial and error, rewarding good outcomes) can teach a model behaviors that are hard to write as rules.

## The problem
Retrieval is reactive: every question starts from scratch, so connections between documents are rediscovered again and again. Knowledge graphs are built with rigid rules that may not fit the questions people actually ask. Both struggle on research-style questions that require stitching facts from many sources. That hurts tools such as research assistants and enterprise search.

## The idea
Picture a librarian who reads a messy archive once, then writes summary sheets, groups related files into folders, and adds "see also" notes. Later visitors find answers quickly. The twist is that the librarian is graded only on whether visitors get correct answers, so it learns which organization actually helps.

## How it works
1. A builder agent (a 4-billion-parameter Qwen3.5 model) sees the raw documents as files in a folder.
2. It takes actions: create a synthetic file that merges sources and links back to them, merge files into a hierarchy, delete its own synthetic files, or stop. Raw documents are never deleted.
3. A separate, frozen answering agent (Qwen3.5-4B or Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) then browses this workspace to answer questions it has never seen.
4. The builder is trained with GRPO (a reinforcement learning method that compares groups of attempts). Its reward is the answerer's accuracy, checked periodically during building and at the end.
5. Training questions are hidden from the builder, so it must anticipate what might be asked rather than memorize it.

## Results
On BrowseComp-Plus, a hard research-question benchmark, accuracy with the Qwen answerer rose to 0.75, versus 0.44 for the best retrieval baseline. With Gemini it reached 0.77, versus 0.36 for GraphRAG (a knowledge-graph method) and 0.28 for the untrained builder. In plain terms, about three in four questions were answered correctly instead of fewer than half.

Building costs tokens up front: about 179,000 per document collection. The authors estimate that across 10 questions per collection, cost per correct answer was 33.8% lower than with the untrained builder.

On BRIGHT, a reasoning-retrieval benchmark the builder never trained on, average first-try accuracy was 52.0%, versus 20.8% for the best baseline. On Stack Overflow questions it hit 85.5% against 11.5%.

The trained builder made far richer structures, about 53 files versus 5 for the untrained one. Shuffling where files were placed lowered accuracy, showing the organization itself matters.

## Why it matters
This shifts effort from answer time to preparation time. Companies with stable document sets, such as manuals or legal archives, could build a workspace once and serve many questions. It also shows that reinforcement learning can teach models to organize memory, not just to answer.

## Caveats
Tests used static document sets; keeping the workspace current as files change is unsolved. The builder must see a large amount of context, which may limit scale. Summaries can drop tiny details, though answerers can follow links back to raw files. The headline 33-point gain depends on which baseline is used; one direct comparison gives 31 points.

## Key terms
- **Retrieval-augmented generation**: fetching relevant text for each question before answering.
- **Knowledge graph**: a precomputed network of facts linking named things.
- **Builder agent**: the model that organizes documents into a workspace.
- **GRPO**: a reinforcement learning method that ranks several attempts against each other.
- **Amortization**: spreading a one-time cost across many later uses.

papers.title: Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?
papers.tldr: Facts taught to unified image-and-text models only through image generation can partly be recalled in text, and interleaved image-text training improves that transfer, but large gaps remain.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper tests whether teaching an AI new facts only through pictures it learns to draw lets it later answer text questions about those facts, and finds the answer is "partly."

## Background you need
A unified multimodal model is one AI that can both understand and generate text and images. Builders hope its two skills share knowledge, so learning in one helps the other. Text-to-image training means showing the model captions paired with images it should learn to produce.

## The problem
Strong scores on separate image and text benchmarks do not prove the knowledge is shared inside the model. If a model can draw a fact but not say it, its "unified" design delivers less than promised. This matters because a lot of world knowledge lives in images, not text. Nobody had a clean way to measure this transfer.

## The idea
Imagine learning a city only from maps you were asked to redraw. Later someone asks, in words, "Is the museum north of the river?" The authors call this "language accessibility": can knowledge picked up visually be retrieved through language? To avoid the model already knowing the answers, they invent a fictional world.

## How it works
1. They create "MagicWorld," a set of made-up entities, each with a hidden attribute such as color, count, shape, size, spatial position, a number or written text. That gives seven categories, with 50 facts each.
2. They train three models (BAGEL, SenseNova-U1 and an in-house GLM-Omni) to generate about 25 images per fact. Captions name the entity but never state the value; only the image shows it.
3. They test with text-only questions, and separately check whether generated images show the right value, using a vision-language model as judge.
4. They try "textual alignment": add a few question-answer examples for half the entities and test on the other half.
5. They try "interleaved alignment": training answers that mix reasoning, a generated image, then a final text answer.

## Results
Direct transfer was weak. Average text accuracy was 8.86% for BAGEL, 14.57% for GLM-Omni, and 20.00% for SenseNova-U1, against a random-guess level of 15.96%. Image accuracy was much higher, from 31.43% to 61.14%. SenseNova-U1 drew numbers correctly 88% of the time but answered them correctly 0% of the time.

Textual alignment helped two models: BAGEL rose to 15.43% and SenseNova-U1 to 28.00%. GLM-Omni dipped slightly to 12.57%. Number and text facts did not transfer to unseen entities at all.

Interleaved alignment did better for all three: 17.14%, 26.86% and 28.57%. For GLM-Omni, shape accuracy jumped from 12% to 64%. Removing the image part of its training dropped GLM-Omni from 26.86% back to 13.71%, so the drawing step matters. Letting models "think with images" at test time raised GLM-Omni to 41.14%.

Correct drawings usually predicted correct answers, but even then the text answer was right less than half the time.

## Why it matters
Image generation can teach a model things text never told it, which is promising for learning from visual data. But today's unified models leave much of that knowledge locked away. Designers get a clear test for measuring how well a model's skills actually connect.

## Caveats
All facts were fictional and synthetic, so real-world images may behave differently. The three models differ in many ways, so the cause of their gaps is not isolated. Some key tests ran on only one model. The paper reports no run-to-run variation or significance tests.

## Key terms
- **Unified multimodal model**: one model that both reads and creates text and images.
- **Language accessibility**: how well visually learned facts can be retrieved in words.
- **Text-to-image training**: teaching a model to draw images from captions.
- **Interleaved alignment**: training answers that mix text reasoning with generated images.
- **Visual chain-of-thought**: having the model draw an image as a reasoning step before answering.
